title: Iterator Pattern
tagline: Traverse any collection sequentially without knowing its internal structure — the foundation of JavaScript's for-of loop.

sections.content:
Imagine you have built a custom binary search tree to store user records sorted by last name. Somewhere else in your codebase, a reporting module needs to walk every record in alphabetical order. The naive approach: expose the tree's internal node structure, write traversal logic directly in the report, and repeat that logic everywhere else that needs alphabetical access. Now imagine switching from a BST to a skip list for performance. Every single traversal site breaks.

This is the core problem the **Iterator** pattern solves. It decouples **how a collection is stored** from **how it is traversed**. The collection provides one thing — a standard traversal interface — and all consumers speak that interface regardless of the underlying structure.

In modern JavaScript, this is not just a design pattern you bolt on — it is a **first-class language protocol**. Any object that implements `[Symbol.iterator]()` becomes an **iterable**: compatible with `for-of`, spread syntax (`...`), destructuring assignment, `Array.from()`, `Promise.all()`, `Map` and `Set` constructors, and every future JS feature that is 'iterable-aware'. **Generator functions** (`function*`) let you produce iterators with zero boilerplate, turning complex lazy sequences into code that reads like a simple loop.

This chapter covers the full picture: the GoF Iterator pattern and its participants, JavaScript's specific iterator and iterable protocols, manual iterator implementation, generator functions and their lazy semantics, infinite sequences, composable generator pipelines, async iterators for paginated APIs and streams, real-world framework usage, and the edge cases and misconceptions that trip up intermediate engineers.

sections.caption: GoF Iterator participants mapped to JavaScript: Iterable = Aggregate, Iterator has next()/return()/throw(), IteratorResult carries { value, done }.

sections.title: The TV Remote and the Channel List
sections.content:
A television stores its channel list internally — maybe sorted by number, maybe grouped by category, maybe stored in a hash map keyed by network name. You, the viewer, never see that internal organisation. You just press **Next Channel** on the remote. Each press delivers the next channel; when you have cycled through all of them, the remote does nothing more (or wraps around).

The **remote** is the Iterator. Its single job is `next()` — give me the next thing, or tell me you are done. The TV's internal data structure is completely hidden. You could swap the channel list from a flat array to a priority-queue sorted by your viewing history, and the remote still works identically.

JavaScript's `for-of` loop is the remote. Your custom data structure — tree, graph, linked list, paginated API, file stream — is the TV. Implementing `[Symbol.iterator]()` is the act of wiring up the remote: once done, the entire JS runtime (spread, destructuring, `Array.from`, `Promise.all`, every library that accepts an iterable) can traverse your collection without knowing or caring how it works inside.

The deeper insight: the remote is **disposable and stateful**. Each time you want a fresh traversal from the beginning, you press 'Menu' again — which in JS terms means calling `[Symbol.iterator]()` again to get a **new** iterator with its own internal cursor position. Multiple remotes can exist simultaneously, each at a different channel.

sections.title: The GoF Iterator Pattern: Problem and Participants
sections.content:
The Gang of Four defined the Iterator pattern in 1994 as a way to 'provide a way to access the elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation.' The four participants are:

**Iterator** — the interface declaring `next()`, `hasNext()`, and optionally `reset()`. In JavaScript, the protocol is `next()` returning `{ value, done }`.

**ConcreteIterator** — implements the Iterator interface for a specific collection. Tracks current position. Is stateful and not thread-safe (in single-threaded JS this is fine, but in Go or Java, each goroutine/thread needs its own iterator instance).

**Aggregate (Iterable)** — the interface declaring `createIterator()`. In JavaScript: `[Symbol.iterator]()`.

**ConcreteAggregate** — your actual collection class. It implements `[Symbol.iterator]()` to return a `ConcreteIterator` initialised to the start of the collection.

The key consequence: client code depends only on the `Iterator` interface, never on `ConcreteAggregate`. You can change the aggregate's internal storage (from array to BST) without touching a single line of traversal code. You can create multiple iterator types over the same aggregate — in-order, pre-order, post-order tree traversal — each a different `ConcreteIterator`.

**JavaScript's specific additions:** The language protocol is richer than the classic GoF definition. An iterator can optionally implement:
- `return(value)` — called when a `for-of` loop exits early via `break` or `return`. Allows resource cleanup (closing a file handle, releasing a DB cursor).
- `throw(error)` — allows injecting an error into a generator from outside, triggering the generator's `try/catch`.

And an object can be **both** iterable and an iterator simultaneously (a self-referential iterator) by returning `this` from `[Symbol.iterator]()`. This is what generators do: the generator object is both.

sequenceDiagram

sections.title: JavaScript's Iterator Protocol in Depth
sections.content:
JavaScript defines two complementary protocols that together form the foundation for all iteration:

**The Iterator Protocol** — An object is an iterator if it has a `next()` method that returns a plain object with exactly two properties: `value` (any JS value) and `done` (a boolean). When `done` is `false`, `value` is the current item. When `done` is `true`, `value` is the optional return value of the sequence (typically `undefined`) and iteration is complete.

**The Iterable Protocol** — An object is iterable if it has a method at the well-known symbol key `Symbol.iterator`. This method takes no arguments and returns an Iterator. Every time you call it, you get a **fresh** iterator starting from the beginning. This is what lets you use an iterable in multiple `for-of` loops without one loop affecting the other.

**Built-in iterables in JavaScript:** `Array`, `String` (iterates Unicode code points, not UTF-16 code units — important for emoji), `Map`, `Set`, `TypedArray` (Int8Array etc.), `NodeList`, `HTMLCollection`, `arguments` object, `URLSearchParams`, `Headers` (fetch API), `FormData`. Notably, plain `{}` objects are **not** iterable by default.

**What consumes iterables:** `for-of` loops, spread syntax in array literals `[...iter]` and function calls `fn(...iter)`, array and object destructuring `const [a, b] = iter`, `Array.from(iter)`, `new Map(iter)`, `new Set(iter)`, `Promise.all(iter)`, `Promise.race(iter)`, `yield*` inside a generator.

**Generators are both:** A generator function returns a Generator object which implements both the Iterator protocol (has `next()`) and the Iterable protocol (has `[Symbol.iterator]()` returning `this`). This means you can spread a generator, use it in `for-of`, pass it to `Array.from` — all without any extra wiring.

**Separate iterator and iterable:** Arrays separate the two. The array itself is the iterable. Calling `arr[Symbol.iterator]()` returns a new `Array Iterator` object — a separate object that is stateful and not the array itself. This means two simultaneous `for-of` loops over the same array maintain independent positions.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: NumberRange is a reusable iterable: each [Symbol.iterator]() call creates a new closure with its own 'current' counter. The countdown object is a self-referential iterator — convenient but single-use. The independence of iter1 and iter2 shows that fresh iterators are truly independent.

sections.title: Generator Functions: Iterators Without the Boilerplate
sections.content:
Writing manual iterators requires careful management of: a `done` flag, a closure to capture state, and a correctly shaped return object. Generator functions eliminate all of that. A `function*` returns a Generator — an object that is both an iterator and an iterable — and the `yield` keyword does all the state management for you.

**How generators work mechanically:** When you call a generator function, it does **not** execute its body. It returns a Generator object immediately. The body only runs when you call `next()` on that object. Execution runs until the first `yield`, emits that value, then **suspends** — pausing the entire call stack, preserving all local variable values. The next `next()` call resumes execution from exactly that suspension point. When the function body returns (or falls off the end), the generator emits `{ value: returnValue, done: true }` and is exhausted.

**`yield` vs `return`:** `yield` suspends and produces `{ value: yielded, done: false }`. `return` (or end of function) produces `{ value: returned, done: true }`. The `value` on the final `done: true` result is often ignored by `for-of` and spread, but is accessible if you call `next()` manually.

**Bidirectional communication:** Generators are not just output devices. The caller can **send values in** by passing an argument to `next(arg)` — the argument becomes the result of the `yield` expression inside the generator. This enables coroutine-like patterns and is how `async/await` is implemented under the hood in older transpilers.

**`yield*` delegation:** Inside a generator, `yield*` followed by any iterable delegates iteration to that iterable, yielding all its values one by one. It is equivalent to `for (const v of iterable) yield v` but more idiomatic. `yield*` also propagates `return()` and `throw()` to the delegated iterator.

**Infinite generators:** Because a generator only produces the next value when `next()` is called, there is no problem writing `while (true)` inside a generator. The Fibonacci generator is infinite — it never runs out of numbers — but consuming only the first 10 values is perfectly safe. No memory explosion, no precomputed array.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: range() is a finite generator replacing the manual NumberRange class in ~3 lines. fibonacci() is infinite but safe — break triggers iterator.return() which cleans up the generator. yield* flatten shows delegation. The accumulator coroutine shows bidirectional communication: yield both emits and receives.

stateDiagram-v2

    SuspendedAtStart --> Running : "next() called"
    Running --> SuspendedAtYield : "yield value"
    SuspendedAtYield --> Running : "next(arg) called"
    Running --> Completed : "return or fall-off"
    SuspendedAtYield --> Completed : "return() or throw()"
    Completed --> [*]

sections.title: Lazy Evaluation: Why It Matters for Performance
sections.content:
The word 'lazy' in computing means: **don't compute a value until it is actually needed**. Iterators are lazy by definition — `next()` is a pull-based model. The consumer asks for one value; the producer computes exactly one value. Nothing is precomputed or buffered.

Contrast this with **eager evaluation**: `array.map(fn)` computes all results immediately and stores them in a new array. For 1 million elements, that is 1 million function calls and 1 million array slots allocated before you can process the first result. If you only need the first 10 results, you wasted the other 999,990 computations.

Lazy iterators enable four important capabilities:

**1. Infinite sequences.** A `range(0, Infinity)` or Fibonacci generator is well-defined and safe. Only the values actually consumed are computed. The generator holds O(1) state — just the current values — regardless of how many values have been produced.

**2. Memory-efficient large dataset processing.** Reading a 10 GB log file line by line with a generator uses O(1) memory — one line in memory at a time. Reading it into an array first would require 10 GB of RAM.

**3. Short-circuit processing.** If you are searching for the first element matching a predicate, a lazy pipeline stops as soon as it finds the match. An eager `filter().find()` chain computes all filtered elements first.

**4. Composable pipelines without intermediate allocations.** Chaining `map`, `filter`, `take` as generator functions creates a pipeline where each value flows through all stages before the next value is pulled. No intermediate arrays are created.

**The tradeoff:** Generators are not always faster than arrays. For small collections where the full result is needed, array methods can be faster due to V8's optimised typed array paths. Generators add function call overhead per value. The win is in scenarios involving large datasets, infinite sequences, or early termination.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A["Source\nfibonacci()"] --> B["map\nx => x*x"]
    B --> C["filter\nx < 100"]
    C --> D["take(5)"]
    D --> E["Result\n[0,1,1,4,25]"]
    style A fill:#e8f4fd
    style E fill:#e8f5e8
sections.caption: Lazy generator pipeline: values flow one-at-a-time through all stages. No intermediate arrays. Pipeline stops when take(5) is satisfied.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The lazy pipeline pulls exactly enough fibonacci values to find 5 perfect squares — never more. The BST in-order traversal is elegant because the generator's own call stack implicitly manages the traversal recursion — something that would require an explicit stack in a manual iterator.

sections.title: Async Iterators: Streams, Files, and Paginated APIs
sections.content:
The iterator protocol extends cleanly to asynchronous data sources via **async iterators**. The protocol is identical but everything is wrapped in Promises:

- An **Async Iterable** has a `[Symbol.asyncIterator]()` method returning an Async Iterator.
- An **Async Iterator** has a `next()` method returning a `Promise<{ value, done }>`.
- `for await...of` is the async counterpart to `for-of`, awaiting each `next()` call.

**Async generator functions** (`async function*`) are the ergonomic way to produce async iterables. Inside, you can `await` promises normally and `yield` values. The consumer's `for await...of` handles all the promise chaining.

**Real use cases:**

**Paginated REST APIs** — Most APIs return data in pages: page 1, page 2, etc. An async generator hides all pagination logic. The consumer iterates items as if they were a flat list. The generator fetches the next page transparently when the previous page is exhausted.

**Node.js Readable Streams** — Since Node.js 10, Readable streams implement `Symbol.asyncIterator`. You can process a multi-gigabyte file with `for await (const chunk of stream)` — memory usage stays constant.

**`readline` interface** — Node.js's `readline.createInterface` returns an async iterable over lines. This is the idiomatic way to process large text files line by line.

**Database cursors** — ORMs and DB drivers (pg-cursor, Mongoose cursor) expose async iterables over query results. Process 10 million rows without loading them all into memory.

**WebSockets and SSE** — A wrapper async generator can yield messages from a WebSocket connection, abstracting the event-listener pattern into a clean iteration model.

**`return()` on async generators:** When `for await...of` exits via `break`, it calls `return()` on the async iterator, which is your chance to close the connection, release the cursor, or abort the fetch.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: paginatedFetch hides all HTTP and pagination complexity — the consumer uses a flat for-await-of loop. readLines wraps readline (itself async iterable) adding a try/finally for cleanup. The finally block in dbCursor runs whether iteration completes normally, breaks early, or throws — the async iterator's return() protocol guarantees this.

sections.caption: Async generator pagination flow: the generator fetches the next page only when the current page is exhausted, triggered by the consumer's next() call.

sections.title: The Iterator Pattern in Real Frameworks and Libraries
sections.content:
Understanding iterators unlocks reading and writing idiomatic code in a broad range of frameworks:

**React:** React's reconciler internally walks fiber trees. `useReducer` is structurally similar to a generator — state machine steps driven by actions. The `useSyncExternalStore` hook can wrap an async iterable source. Third-party libraries like `react-query`'s infinite query use paginated cursor patterns identical to the async generator approach.

**Node.js Streams:** Transform streams implement both readable and writable interfaces. Since Node 10, Readable streams implement `[Symbol.asyncIterator]`, so you can `for await...of` a stream directly. `pipeline()` composes streams the way generator pipelines compose synchronous iterators.

**Lodash / Ramda:** Lodash's `_.chain()` is an eager pipeline. Libraries like `lazy.js` and `iter-tools` provide lazy equivalents using iterators. ES2025's `Iterator.prototype` built-in methods (`.map()`, `.filter()`, `.take()`) are standardising exactly this pattern natively.

**RxJS Observables:** Observables are push-based (the producer controls timing) while iterators are pull-based (consumer controls timing). Both model sequences over time, but the Iterator is synchronous-pull and Observable is async-push. `from(iterable)` converts any iterable to an Observable. `toArray()` converts an Observable back. Understanding one makes the other much easier.

**Database ORMs:** TypeORM's `QueryBuilder` supports streaming via cursors. Prisma's `findMany` with `cursor` pagination follows the cursor pattern. Mongoose's `.cursor()` returns an async iterable. All of these are the Iterator pattern applied to database access.

**Native JS Iterator Helpers (Stage 4 / ES2025):** The TC39 proposal adds `.map()`, `.filter()`, `.take()`, `.drop()`, `.flatMap()`, `.reduce()`, `.forEach()`, `.some()`, `.every()`, `.find()`, `.toArray()` directly to all iterator objects via `Iterator.prototype`. This means you will soon be able to write `fibonacci().filter(isPrime).take(10).toArray()` natively.

**Python comparison:** Python's `__iter__` / `__next__` protocol is directly analogous. Python's `yield` works identically. The key difference: Python generators return `StopIteration` exception (not a `{ done: true }` value) to signal exhaustion — a design choice JavaScript deliberately avoided for performance reasons.

sections.title: Edge Cases, Misconceptions, and Gotchas
sections.content:
Several iterator behaviours consistently surprise developers:

**1. Generators are single-use iterators.** A generator object can only be iterated once. Once `done: true`, it stays done. If you want to iterate again, call the generator function again for a new Generator object. Classes that implement `[Symbol.iterator]()` can be iterated multiple times because each call returns a new, independent iterator.

**2. `for-of` vs `for-in`.** `for-of` iterates **values** of an iterable (uses the iterator protocol). `for-in` iterates **enumerable property keys** of any object (uses a completely different mechanism, includes prototype chain properties). Never use `for-in` on arrays — it iterates string indices plus any enumerable properties on `Array.prototype` that have been added by libraries.

**3. `done: true` value is ignored by `for-of`.** When a generator `return`s a value — e.g., `return 'finished'` — the IteratorResult `{ value: 'finished', done: true }` is produced. But `for-of` and spread ignore this terminal value. Only manually calling `next()` until `done: true` will see it. If you need the return value, use a manual `while` loop with `iter.next()`.

**4. Early exit and resource cleanup.** When `for-of` breaks early, it calls `iterator.return()` if that method exists. Generator functions automatically implement `return()` — the `finally` block runs. Manual iterators must implement `return()` explicitly if they hold resources. Failure to do so causes resource leaks.

**5. `String` iterates Unicode code points, not code units.** `'hello'[0]` gives `'h'` (index access, code unit). `[...'hello'][0]` gives `'h'` too — but `[...'\uD83D\uDE00'][0]` gives the full emoji `'😀'` (one code point), not just the surrogate half `'\uD83D'`. String iteration is emoji-safe; index access is not.

**6. Passing an iterable vs an iterator.** If you pass an iterator (not an iterable) to a function that calls `[Symbol.iterator]()`, it works because generators return `this` from `[Symbol.iterator]()`. But a plain manual iterator object without `[Symbol.iterator]()` will throw `TypeError: obj is not iterable`. Always implement both protocols if your object will be consumed by iterable-aware APIs.

**7. Async iterator cleanup.** `for await...of` calls `return()` on the async iterator when breaking. But if you call the async generator's `next()` manually and stop without calling `return()`, the `finally` block may never run. Always use `for await...of` or explicitly call `return()` when done.

**How `async/await` is built on generators:** Before native `async/await` existed in JavaScript, Babel transpiled it using generators. An `async` function becomes a generator function; `await` becomes `yield`. A runtime helper (`co`, `regenerator-runtime`) drives the generator: it calls `next()`, receives a Promise, `.then()`-s it, and calls `next(resolvedValue)` when the Promise resolves. The bidirectional `next(value)` protocol — where the caller can send a value back into the generator — is what makes this work. Understanding generators makes `async/await` feel less magical and helps diagnose edge cases in error propagation and cancellation.

**When to use the Iterator pattern:**
- Custom data structures that clients need to traverse (trees, graphs, linked lists, tries)
- Lazy or infinite sequences where materialising the full collection is impractical
- Streaming large datasets from files, databases, or network without loading all into memory
- Paginated API consumption where the consumer should not manage page tokens
- Multiple traversal strategies over the same collection (in-order / pre-order / breadth-first)

**When NOT to use it:**
- For plain arrays you own: use built-in `.map()`, `.filter()`, `.reduce()` — they are faster and more readable
- For simple one-off transformations: a regular function returning an array is fine
- When you need random access (index into position N in O(1)): iterators are sequential only
- When the collection is small and fully known: lazy evaluation overhead outweighs benefits

**Always prefer `function*` over manual iterators** — generators handle `return()` cleanup automatically via `finally`, eliminate manual `done` flag management, and are significantly more readable. Manual iterators are warranted only when you need a custom `return()` method for non-generator resource cleanup.

**Native Iterator Helpers coming:** ES2025 `Iterator.prototype.map/filter/take` will eliminate custom pipeline helpers. Write generator functions now; the native helpers will be drop-in replacements.

items: **Iterator pattern** decouples collection traversal from storage structure. Clients depend only on `next()` → `{ value, done }`, never on internal implementation details.

**JavaScript's iterable protocol** — `[Symbol.iterator]()` returning an Iterator — makes any object compatible with `for-of`, spread, destructuring, `Array.from`, and all iterable-aware APIs. Built-ins (Array, String, Map, Set) are already iterable; plain objects are not.

**Generators** (`function*` + `yield`) produce iterators automatically with zero boilerplate. They suspend execution at each `yield`, preserving all local state, and resume on the next `next()` call — enabling infinite sequences and lazy pipelines without manual state management.

**Lazy evaluation** means values are computed only when pulled. This enables: O(1) memory for infinite sequences, early-exit short-circuiting, composable pipelines with no intermediate array allocations, and memory-efficient large dataset processing.

**`yield*`** delegates iteration to another iterable, and **`next(value)`** sends values back into a generator — enabling coroutine patterns and underpinning how async/await was implemented before native support.

**Async iterators** (`async function*` + `for await...of`) extend the protocol to asynchronous sources. Use them for paginated APIs, Node.js streams, database cursors, and WebSocket message streams — always implement `finally` for resource cleanup.

**Key gotchas:** generators are single-use; `for-of` ignores the `done: true` terminal value; `String` iteration is Unicode-code-point-safe (emoji-safe) while index access is not; always implement both Iterator and Iterable protocols if exposing objects to iterable-aware APIs.

quiz.question: What must an object implement to be considered an 'iterable' in JavaScript?
options: A forEach() method that accepts a callback.
A [Symbol.iterator]() method that returns an object with a next() method.
A next() method directly on the object itself.
Extending the built-in Array class.
quiz.explanation: The iterable protocol requires [Symbol.iterator]() — a method at the Symbol.iterator key — that returns an Iterator (an object with next() returning { value, done }). Having next() directly on the object makes it an Iterator, not an Iterable. forEach() is unrelated to the protocol.

quiz.question: What does the `yield` keyword do inside a generator function?
options: Throws an error to signal the end of the sequence.
Returns the final value and marks the generator as done.
Suspends execution, emits a value as { value, done: false }, and resumes on the next next() call.
Creates a new generator object with a cloned state.
quiz.explanation: yield pauses the generator at that exact point, emits { value: yielded, done: false }, and saves the entire call stack. The next call to next() resumes from right after the yield. This suspension-resume cycle is what enables lazy, stateful sequences.

quiz.question: What is returned by iterator.next() when the sequence is fully exhausted?
options: null
undefined
{ value: undefined, done: true }
{ value: null, done: false }
quiz.explanation: The iterator protocol specifies { value: undefined, done: true } (or any value with done === true) to signal exhaustion. The for-of loop and spread operator stop consuming when they see done: true and discard the terminal value.

quiz.question: Why is lazy evaluation the key performance advantage of iterators over materialised arrays?
options: Iterators cache computed values automatically, so repeated access is faster.
Iterators only compute the next value when next() is called, enabling infinite sequences and avoiding loading large datasets into memory.
Iterators execute all transformations in parallel using Web Workers.
Iterators skip JavaScript's garbage collector by using typed arrays internally.
quiz.explanation: An infinite Fibonacci generator holds only two numbers (a, b) in memory regardless of how many values have been produced. A materialised array of infinite Fibonacci numbers is impossible. For finite but large datasets, lazy iterators avoid the O(n) memory cost of materialisation.

quiz.question: You call [Symbol.iterator]() on an array twice and assign each result to a different variable. What happens when you call next() on each independently?
options: Both iterators share the same cursor position — advancing one advances the other.
The second call to [Symbol.iterator]() throws an error because the array is already being iterated.
Each call returns a new, independent iterator with its own cursor position starting at 0.
The second iterator starts from where the first left off.
quiz.explanation: Each call to [Symbol.iterator]() creates a fresh Array Iterator object with its own internal index starting at 0. The two iterators are fully independent — advancing one has no effect on the other. This is the correct design: [Symbol.iterator]() is a factory.

quiz.question: What does `yield*` do inside a generator function?
options: Yields a Promise and awaits its resolution before continuing.
Delegates iteration to another iterable, yielding all of its values one by one.
Terminates the generator immediately and returns the iterable as the final value.
Creates a nested generator scope with its own this binding.
quiz.explanation: yield* iterable is equivalent to for (const v of iterable) yield v, but it also propagates return() and throw() to the delegated iterator. It is the idiomatic way to compose generators — for example, flattening nested iterables or recursing in tree traversal.

quiz.question: When a for-of loop exits early via break, what happens to the iterator?
options: The iterator's next() method is called one final time with a special sentinel value.
The iterator's return() method is called, allowing cleanup code in a generator's finally block to run.
The iterator is garbage collected immediately without any cleanup.
The loop throws a BreakException that the iterator must catch.
quiz.explanation: The for-of loop calls iterator.return() when it exits early (via break, return, or throw). Generator functions implement return() automatically: the generator resumes inside any active finally block, giving you a chance to close file handles, release DB cursors, or clean up other resources.

quiz.question: What is the correct pattern for consuming a paginated REST API where the consumer should not manage page tokens?
options: Use Promise.all() to fetch all pages in parallel, then flatten the results.
Use an async generator (async function*) that fetches the next page when the previous is exhausted, yielding individual items — consumed with for await...of.
Use Array.from() with an async mapping function and the total item count.
Use a regular generator with fetch() calls inside, relying on the event loop.
quiz.explanation: async function* is the idiomatic pattern: the generator hides pagination (page tokens, hasMore flags) entirely. The consumer uses for await...of and sees a flat stream of items. break triggers return() which can abort any in-flight fetch. Using Promise.all() would fetch all pages eagerly, potentially making thousands of requests.

quiz.question: Which statement about iterating a String with for-of vs bracket index access is correct?
options: Both for-of and index access return UTF-16 code units, so they behave identically.
for-of iterates Unicode code points (emoji-safe), while index access returns UTF-16 code units (may split emoji into surrogates).
Index access iterates Unicode code points; for-of returns raw bytes.
for-of can only iterate ASCII strings; index access handles full Unicode.
quiz.explanation: JavaScript strings are stored as UTF-16. Emoji and characters above U+FFFF are encoded as surrogate pairs (two code units). String[Symbol.iterator]() iterates code points — one full emoji per iteration. Index access returns individual code units — splitting an emoji into two unusable surrogate halves.

quiz.question: When should you NOT implement [Symbol.iterator] on a custom object?
options: When the object represents a custom linked list where order matters.
When the object represents a database cursor that fetches rows lazily.
When the object is a configuration object or service class that does not represent a sequence.
When the object's values need to be consumed by Array.from().
quiz.explanation: KISS and YAGNI: iterability signals 'this object represents a sequence of values that can be traversed one at a time.' A config object { timeout: 5000, retries: 3 } is not a sequence — adding [Symbol.iterator] is misleading and violates the principle of least surprise. A service class is also not a sequence. Only add iterability when sequential traversal is genuinely the primary use case.
